explanations.answer: No rain yet and no man to work the ground
explanations.explanation: Right on, friend. Verse 5 gives two reasons: the LORD God had not yet sent rain upon the earth, and there was no man to cultivate the ground. Two things missing, and the field is just waiting. It's like a mixer with no dough and nobody to turn it on. Plenty of potential and zero cookies.

explanations.answer: The waters still cover all the dry land
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think that, but the waters were already gathered and the dry land had already appeared (Genesis 1:9-10). So the ground is out in the open here. The reason verse 5 gives is different: no rain yet, and no man to cultivate the ground.

explanations.answer: The sun has not been set in the sky
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since plants do love sunshine. But God had already set lights in the expanse of the sky (Genesis 1:14-17), and this verse doesn't mention them at all. What it says is that the LORD God had not yet sent rain, and there was no man to cultivate the ground.

explanations.answer: Springs well up from the earth
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Verse 6 says springs welled up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground. No rain, no problem. The water came up from below instead of down from above, and that's a plot twist I did not see coming.

explanations.answer: Dew settles on it every morning
explanations.explanation: Dew sounds so peaceful, doesn't it? The passage never mentions it, though. What verse 6 says is that springs welled up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground.

Nice thinking, friend, but snow and mountains don't show up in this passage. Verse 6 keeps it simple: springs welled up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground. The water comes from the earth itself.
Dust, baker! Verse 7 says the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground. Think about that for a second. I spent years under dust in a drawer and never once became anything but dusty.
Stones are tough, I'll give you that. But verse 7 says the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground. Dust is the word the text uses, so that's the one that fits the blank.

Roots would make sense in a garden story, friend. But verse 5 says no plant had even sprouted yet, so there's nothing with roots around. Verse 7 says the LORD God formed man from the dust of the ground.
True, baker! Verse 7 says the LORD God breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being. The breath came from God Himself. That's where the man's life starts.

This one is true, friend. Verse 7 says the LORD God formed the man from the dust, breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and the man became a living being. So the statement on the card matches the text exactly.
True! Verse 9 says that out of the ground the LORD God gave growth to every tree that is pleasing to the eye and good for food. Pretty to look at and good to eat. That's a garden doing its job.
This one is true, friend. Verse 9 says that out of the ground the LORD God gave growth to every tree that is pleasing to the eye and good for food. So the card matches the text word for word.

That's the one, baker! Verse 15 says the LORD God placed him in the Garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it. The man has real work to do. I respect that, because a job with a purpose beats a spot in a drawer any day.

explanations.answer: To build a city in the east
explanations.explanation: The east is in the passage, friend, since the garden is planted in Eden, in the east (verse 8). But nothing here talks about a city. Verse 15 says the man is placed in the garden to cultivate and keep it.

explanations.answer: To hunt the beasts of the field
explanations.explanation: The beasts of the field do show up later in the passage. But when verse 19 gets to them, the LORD God brings them to the man to see what he would name each one. Hunting isn't mentioned. His job in verse 15 is to cultivate and keep the garden.

Close, but that's a flip of what the text says. The LORD God tells the man, “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden,” and that's every tree, not just one. The limit comes in the next verse, and it's on one tree only (Genesis 2:16-17).
Right, baker! The LORD God says, “You may eat freely from every tree of the garden,” (Genesis 2:16). That's a whole garden of yes. Only one tree gets a no, and that comes in verse 17.

explanations.answer: The tree of the knowledge of good and evil
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker! The LORD God says, “but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil…” (Genesis 2:17). Out of a whole garden, one tree gets that warning. That tree stands in the middle of the garden next to the tree of life, which is why I told you to keep your eye on both.

explanations.answer: The tree of life in the middle of the garden
explanations.explanation: That tree is in the middle of the garden, friend, but it isn't the one named in the warning. The LORD God says, “but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil…” (Genesis 2:17). Easy to mix up, since the two trees stand together.

explanations.answer: The tamarisk tree planted at Beersheba
explanations.explanation: That tree is a long way from Eden, friend. It's planted later by Abraham, a man God calls later in Genesis (Genesis 21:33). In the garden, the LORD God says, “but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil…” (Genesis 2:17).
True, baker. The LORD God says, “…for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.” It's a clear warning, and it comes with the command. I think a warning like that is a serious thing to hear.

This one is true, friend. In verse 17 the LORD God says, “…for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.” So the card matches the text. It's a clear warning that comes right with the command.

explanations.answer: For the man to be alone
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The LORD God says, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” Think about it. The garden is full of trees and rivers, and the one thing the LORD God points to is that the man is by himself.

explanations.answer: For the rivers to run dry
explanations.explanation: The rivers are flowing just fine in this passage, friend. A river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and then it branches into four (verses 10-14). What the LORD God calls not good is, “It is not good for the man to be alone.”

explanations.answer: For the animals to roam untamed
explanations.explanation: The animals do come up next, friend, but nothing here calls them untamed. The LORD God says, “It is not good for the man to be alone.” That's the thing He names.
Helper, baker! The LORD God says, “I will make for him a suitable helper.” Notice the word suitable. It's not just any helper, it's one who fits. That's like the right lid for the right canister.
Shelter makes sense for somebody alone, friend. But that's not the word in the text. The LORD God says, “I will make for him a suitable helper.”
A throne would be fancy, friend, but nothing in this passage mentions one. When the LORD God sees the man alone, He says, “I will make for him a suitable helper.” That's the word for the blank.

explanations.answer: To see what he would name each one
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker! Verse 19 says the LORD God brought them to the man to see what he would name each one. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. I would still be stuck on the first one, changing my mind.

explanations.answer: To teach him how to care for them
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a good reason, friend, but the text doesn't give it. Verse 19 says the LORD God brought them to the man to see what he would name each one. I'll stick to the reason the passage gives.

explanations.answer: To let him pick which ones to keep
explanations.explanation: Picking favorites would be a fun job, friend, but it isn't in the text. Verse 19 says the LORD God brought the beasts and the birds to the man to see what he would name each one. Naming is the whole point of that moment.

Not quite, friend. Verse 20 says the man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the air, and to every beast of the field. Then it says that for Adam no suitable helper was found. So he named them all and none of them was the match.

That's right, baker! The man named all the livestock, the birds of the air, and every beast of the field. But verse 20 says that for Adam no suitable helper was found. A whole parade, and not one match.

A rib, baker! Verse 21 says that while the man slept, the LORD God took one of the man's ribs and closed up the area with flesh. The man was in a deep sleep the whole time. I think that's one sleep nobody could complain about.
Hair is a fun guess, friend, but the text doesn't mention it. Verse 21 says the LORD God took one of the man's ribs while he slept. Then He closed up the area with flesh.
That's a creative one, friend, but blood isn't in the passage. Verse 21 says the LORD God took one of the man's ribs while he slept and closed up the area with flesh. A rib is what the text names.

Woman, baker! Verse 22 says that from the rib the LORD God had taken from the man, He made a woman and brought her to him. The rib comes first, and then the woman is brought to the man. That's the answer to the helper the LORD God promised.
A child isn't in the text, friend. Verse 22 says that from the rib the LORD God had taken from the man, He made a woman and brought her to him. Woman is the word that fits the blank.

Servant isn't the word the text uses, friend. Verse 22 says that from the rib the LORD God had taken, He made a woman and brought her to the man. The LORD God had promised a suitable helper, and the passage says woman.

explanations.answer: Because she was taken out of man
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker! The man says, “she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.” He gives the reason himself. The name fits where she came from.

explanations.answer: Because she would rule over the animals
explanations.explanation: The animals are in the passage, but the man never says that. His reason is, “she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.” Nothing about ruling anything.

explanations.answer: Because God gave her that name
explanations.explanation: Close, but look at who is speaking, friend. It's the man who says, “she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.” The reason comes straight from him, and it's about where she was taken from.

True, baker! Verse 24 says, “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife…” It's the same thing the text says. The reason it points back to is what just happened with the man and the woman.

This one is true, friend. Verse 24 says, “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife…” So the card matches the text. I just wanted to make sure the verse had its say.
